Chapter 6. Information As Power: Who Knows What, and Why It Matters.
There’s this quiet tension that runs beneath every negotiation, every transaction, every single moment when two people want different things. It’s the tension of information—who has it, who doesn’t, and how it gets used. Most of us don’t realize just how much of our lives are shaped by these hidden imbalances.
Imagine a young couple, a little nervous but excited, stepping into a car dealership. Maybe they’ve done some homework, checked a few numbers, but the salesperson? They know the real bottom line—the lowest price the dealership will accept, those hidden fees, and the subtle tricks that can nudge a buyer into spending more. The couple tries to bargain, but you can see it—the real advantage belongs to the person with more information.
This pattern shows up everywhere. Think about insurance: companies set rates using mountains of data, way more than the average customer could ever see. Or job interviews—employers quietly gather clues about a candidate’s background, while the applicant is left guessing what the company truly wants. Even dating’s not immune—people put forward their best versions, holding back details until they feel it’s safe to share.
Here’s a story that really brings this to life. Picture a group of real estate agents. When they’re selling their own homes, they keep the property on the market longer, holding out for higher offers. Why? Because they know all the tricks, and they use their inside knowledge to benefit themselves. But when they’re selling for clients, it’s different—they’re more likely to accept the first decent offer, eager to close the deal and move on. It’s not just about the money—it’s about who holds the cards.
But here’s the thing: information doesn’t always stay hidden forever. The internet has totally changed the game. Now, it’s easier than ever to compare prices, read reviews, and learn from others’ experiences. Buyers can walk into that same dealership armed with data. Job seekers can research companies before the interview. The balance of power is shifting, even if the dance of information keeps going.
So, what’s the lesson here? The more you know, the better your choices get. But there’s almost always someone who knows a little more. The smartest players? They’re the ones who spot those gaps—and work to close them.
